// The names of SLUS_006.28, by address. This file is the register: the one place
// that says what each named symbol is called, where the name came from and what
// backs it. recipe/compile.py reads the `name = 0xADDRESS;` part; the rest of a
// row is for people. docs/naming.md has the rules in full.
//
// A function or datum with NO row here is named for its address (func_80012345,
// D_800B1234): nothing is claimed about it. A row whose name IS an address is
// here for what it says after the `//`: a note, or `was:`, a name it once had
// that was taken away because nothing backed it. A row whose name is not its
// address carries:
//
//   type:  size:   what the first split recorded
//   src:           where the name came from
//       sdk-bytes  its bytes are a member of Sony's library, in the release this
//                  program links, outside the fields the linker fills; the name
//                  is Sony's symbol
//       sdk-link   a member proven that way calls it by this name
//       sdk-later  it is part of a member proven that way, which gives it no public
//                  name; a LATER release of Sony's libraries exports the identical
//                  bytes under this name. Not what the linked release calls it:
//                  what a later one does.
//       sdk-earlier  it is part of a member proven that way, which gives it no
//                  public name; an EARLIER release exports the identical bytes
//                  under this name (psx_psyq_signatures). Not what the linked
//                  release calls it: what an earlier one did.
//       sdk-text   it is part of a member proven that way, and Sony's own text in
//                  that member names it: a string it prints begins with the name,
//                  or a message of the member names it as the function it calls
//       original   the developers' own name: the function's own assertion message
//                  begins with it, or its own debug print does and the values in
//                  the print's parentheses are the function's own arguments
//       port       Eternal Silver's name for its transcription      (none yet)
//       public-source  a function of a published source file that the developers
//                  compiled into the program: the same parameters, and the published
//                  body statement by statement. The row names the file and lists what
//                  the program's copy leaves out or replaces
//       coined     given here, by reading the C; the row says what was read
//       inherited  came with the first split or its auto-naming and has not been
//                  read since. NOT evidence of what the function does.
//   on:            the day the name, or its source, was recorded
//   was:           every name it had before, newest first. A citation by an old
//                  name is resolved here, not in a version history.
//   ev:            the evidence, to the end of the line
//
// Nothing checks this file yet (docs/naming.md, "What is not checked"). Until
// something does: a function's address is its identity, so cite it by address,
// or by name with the address beside it.

g_BgSlotBlocks = 0x1F800000; // type:data src:coined on:2026-10-14 was:D_1F800000 ev: read in bg_tile.c: a word of the game's own in the CPU's scratchpad, 16 signed 16-bit words (0x20 bytes to g_BgAttributeSlotBlocks), one for each of the 16 slots of 64 words of tile_lookup_table: the number of the bg's block of 8 x 8 tiles that the slot holds, -1 for none. bg_data_reset and bg_slot_reset store -1 in all 16; bg_block_load stores the block's number (tx >> 3) + (ty >> 3) * 16 in its slot's word, slot ((tx >> 3) & 3) | ((ty >> 1) & 0xC), before it fills the slot; bg_tile_set stores -1 in the slot of a block it has changed; bg_first_draw and bg_copy compare the word with the block they want and call bg_block_load when it is another. The C reaches it as an extern array the linker places at the address (an automatic count finds no use; the task's list has 7). The rows of all six and the C's comment above bg_first_draw ('the s16 at g_BgSlotBlocks[slot] names the page each slot holds') read it the same way. The twin of the first wave's g_BgAttributeSlotBlocks, whose row suggests this name: Bg as the bg_ functions, SlotBlocks: by slot, the block

exception_address_patch = 0x8001B058; // type:func src:coined on:2026-10-13 was:func_8001B058 ev: read in exception.c: writes a 32-bit address into a pair of instruction words that load it in two halves. Arguments: the address of the first of the two words, and the value. The value's lower 16 bits go into the low half of the second word; its upper 16 bits go into the low half of the first, plus 1 when bit 15 of the value is set, because the second instruction adds its half as a signed number. It returns the upper half as stored. It reads no global and calls nothing. Three jumps reach it: two in exception_handler_set and one in exception_hook_set, for the pairs at g_ExceptionHandlerWords, g_ExceptionHandlerWords + 0xB0 and g_ExceptionHookWords. exception_handler_set = 0x8001B07C; // type:func src:coined on:2026-10-13 was:func_8001B07C ev: read in exception.c: makes ready the instructions that run when the hook has caught an exception. It calls exception_address_patch twice: the address g_ExceptionRegisters goes into the instruction pair at g_ExceptionHandlerWords, and its own argument into the pair at g_ExceptionHandlerWords + 0xB0. The words at g_ExceptionHandlerWords in the image are instructions (decoded from the image for this row): after the first pair they store the processor's 32 registers at offsets 0 to 0x7C from the address filled in, then three registers of the system coprocessor, numbers 14, 13 and 8 (where the exception happened, its cause, the address that could not be used), at 0x94, 0x90 and 0x8C; they copy the first address into the first argument register, and after the second pair they jump to the address filled in there. So g_ExceptionRegisters is where the registers are saved, and the argument is the routine then run with that address as its argument: the handler. Its one call is in exception_hook_set, which passes its own argument on. Nothing else in the image forms the address g_ExceptionRegisters or g_ExceptionHandlerWords (measured)

It stores the frames in both g_ScreenFadeFramesLeft (the frames left) and g_ScreenFadeLength (the length), the mode in the byte g_ScreenFadeMode, and 0xFF in the three 16-bit colour words g_ScreenFadeColByte0, g_ScreenFadeColByte1 and g_ScreenFadeColByte2. screen_fade_step makes the fade from these, one frame at a call: bit 1 of the mode picks whether the screen goes toward black or toward white, bit 0 whether the fade grows or dies away. Only this function and screen_fade_step touch the six (measured in the image). Seven jumps from four functions: StartPictureShow (start_picture.c), PictureShow (picture.c) and StartScreenShow (start_screen.c) each pass (0x20, 2) first and (0x20, 3) later, on either side of the frames in which they show a picture; StartMenuRun (start_screen.c) passes (0, 0), after which screen_fade_step draws nothing
screen_fade_step = 0x8001C0F0; // type:func src:coined on:2026-10-13 was:func_8001C0F0 ev: read in screen_fade.c: one frame of the screen fade that screen_fade_start set going. With no frames left (g_ScreenFadeFramesLeft is 0) it does nothing. Otherwise it works out a strength for each of the three colour words (0xFF each): 0xFF * k / length, the division through value_div (map_look.c), where k is the frames left when bit 0 of the mode byte g_ScreenFadeMode is clear, so that the strength dies away, and length - frames left - 1 when it is set, so that it grows; on the last frame of a growing fade the strength is the whole 0xFF. A strength below 0 is made 0. Then it covers the screen with one flat rectangle of 320 x 224 at ordering-table entry 8, through packet_box_add (packet_shape.c). With bit 1 of the mode clear the rectangle is semi-transparent in that colour and is followed by the draw-mode packet 0x220 from packet_tpage_add; with bit 1 set, the same with draw mode 0x240, or, at full strength, a plain black rectangle and no draw-mode packet. Bits 5 and 6 of the GPU's draw mode say how a semi-transparent packet is laid on the screen: 1 (0x20) adds its colour, 2 (0x40) takes it away (from this reader's knowledge of the GPU, not from the C). So mode 2 brings the screen up out of black and mode 3 takes it down to black, the two modes the callers of screen_fade_start use. Last it takes 1 from the frames left. Three callers: MessageShadeDraw (message_draw.c) calls it after a rectangle of its own, StartPictureStep (start_picture.c) after three sprites that cover the screen, and PictureStep (picture.c) in each frame of a picture's show

tile_layer_draw = 0x8001D4E0; // type:func src:coined on:2026-10-13 was:func_8001D4E0 ev: read in tile_layer.c: draws the tile layer. Its two arguments are the scroll position in pixels (x, y). For 15 rows, and for columns 0 to 0x14 (-2 to 0x18 with the wave on: g_TileWaveShown and g_TileWaveSize both not 0, after one call of tile_wave_strips_make), it reads the tile word of cell (column + (x >> 4), row + (y >> 4)) through tile_cell_get. The word 0xFFFF is an empty cell and is passed over, or drawn as word 0 when g_TileEmptyFillOn is not 0. Any other word is drawn as a 16 x 16-pixel tile at (column * 16 - (x & 15), row * 16 - (y & 15)): texel u = (word & 0xF) * 16, v = word & 0xF0, and bits 0x4000 and 0x8000 mirror it across and down. Each packet is written by hand at the packet write pointer g_PacketWritePointer and linked at the head of entry 0x300 of the ordering table (base in g_PacketOtBase): with the wave on, one textured four-cornered polygon (code 0x2C) for each of the three strips at g_TileWaveStrips whose row count is not 0; with it off, one such polygon for a mirrored tile, and a draw-mode word (0xE1000200 | texture page) with a 16 x 16 sprite (code 0x7C) for any other. The colour is the word g_TileCol; g_TileSemiTransOn not 0 sets the semi-transparency bit of the packet's code and bit 0x20 of its texture page word. The texture page word and the palette come from g_TileTPages and g_TileCluts by the number ((g_TileTPageFirst - 0x19) / 2 + 4 + the word's bit 0x100) | 0x20; with g_TileTPageFirst at 0x19, the only value the program stores there, that is texture page word 0x99 or 0x9B and palette 0x7D40 in the image. Its one call is in tile_layer_step. bg_first_draw (bg_tile.c) draws the map's 16 x 16 tiles out of the same table with the same u, v and mirror bits. docs/spec/code/subsystems/rendering.md and docs/spec/assets/battle-effects.md read it the same way

Four arguments: mask, length in frames, one that is not read, and the address of three 16-bit numbers. In a record so named the step number (+0) becomes 1, the length (+2) is stored, the start (+4) takes the old target (+0x10), the target takes the new numbers and the difference (+0x16) is target less start. Bit 4, the record at g_LayerBgFirstRecord: three channels, each target passed through layer_col_conv. Bit 0x80, the record at g_LayerFlatRecord: three channels, each target cut to 0 to 0xFF as it stands. Bit 8, the record at g_LayerBgSecondRecord, and bit 0x100, the record at g_LayerSpriteRecord: the first number only, through layer_col_conv. The start is the last target, not the value the record has now. The image holds 1 jump to it, in layer_col_fade_start; the C writes the call in each of the four arms of that function's switch

The record at g_LayerFlatRecord (three channels) is only stepped. The records at g_LayerBgSecondRecord and g_LayerSpriteRecord (one value each) are followed by layer_col_apply(8) and layer_col_apply(0x100) when g_BtlRunning is 0. pad_update = 0x8001F508; // type:func src:coined on:2026-10-13 was:func_8001F508 ev: read in pad_update.c: the pad's work for one frame, in two parts. First it steps a list of commands for the controller's two actuators, whose address is in g_PadActuatorList (0 for none). A command byte's high four bits say what to do and its bit 0 which actuator: set the level (0x10), the upper and the lower limit (0x20, 0x30), the way the level moves (0x40), the frames between moves (0x50) or the size of a move (0x80); put an actuator back to rest (0x70, 0x90); wait a count of frames (0x60) or until the word g_MovieFrameNumber reaches a value (0xA0); go round a stretch a number of times (0xC0, 0xB0); a byte of 0 ends the list. While a wait runs, each actuator's level, a byte at g_PadActuatorLevels, is moved in its way: to 0, up or down by the step as far as a limit, from one limit to the other, or by a random amount taken with rng_draw. Bits of g_PadActuatorRestFlags ask for the actuators to be put to rest before a list and after it, and both levels are made 0 when byte 5 of the block g_GameOptions points at is 0. Second, for port 0x10 and then port 0, Sony's PadGetState and PadInfoMode(port, 1, 0): for a controller of kind 4 or 7 the two button bytes of the port's buffer (g_PadPort10Buffer or g_PadPort00Buffer, the two PadInitDirect was given) make a 16-bit word; on kinds 5 and 7 a byte 6 or 7 of the buffer below 0x50 or from 0xB1 up clears one of the bits 0x8000, 0x2000, 0x1000 and 0x4000, as a button held down does; and when any bit is clear the word, inverted, becomes g_PadButtons. A controller of kind 7 is also sent the two levels with PadSetAct, and PadSetActAlign with the bytes at g_PadActuatorAlignBytes when its state is 6. Last it counts in D_800B89FC the frames since a button was down, copies g_PadButtons to g_PadPreviousButtons and sets g_PadPressedButtons to the buttons that are down now and were not the frame before. Its one caller is pad_frame_step, which does nothing else and is called by frame_end at every frame's end and by cd_status_get

pad_press_repeat = 0x80023070; // type:func src:coined on:2026-10-13 was:func_80023070 ev: read in overlay.c: makes buttons that stay held count as pressed again. It takes no argument, calls nothing and returns nothing. It compares the buttons held, g_PadButtons, with the copy of them it kept at its last call, g_PadPressRepeatPreviousButtons. Equal and not 0: the count g_PadPressRepeatWait goes down by g_FrameVSyncCount and, when it falls below 0, the held buttons are written into the pressed word g_PadPressedButtons and the count is put back to 4. Not equal: when no button is held the count is set to 0x20, and the copy is brought up to date. BtlRoundStatusUpdate = 0x800297A4; // type:func src:coined on:2026-10-13 was:func_800297A4 ev: read in btl_round.c: what the statuses do at the start of a round; takes no argument. (1) BtlActionOutcomeClear (btl_target.c) zeroes per-slot bytes and words of the round (g_BtlSlotAmountKinds, g_BtlSlotFallMarks, g_BtlSlotAmounts and others). (2) For each of the 14 slots that is active and has a status byte (+0x15 of its stats) that is not 0, four of its bits are counted toward their end, each with a byte counter of its own for the slot: 0x04 with g_BtlSlotStatus4Rounds (not in battle number 0xF9), 0x08 with g_BtlSlotStatus8Rounds, 0x40 with g_BtlSlotStatus40Rounds and 0x80 with g_BtlSlotStatus80Rounds. The counter goes up by 1 and BtlStatusWearOffCheck(counter) is asked; on a yes the bit is flipped off and the counter set to 0, and for 0x08 on a party slot the bit 0x04 of the stats' +0x1E is cleared too. BtlStatusWearOffCheck answers yes when rng_draw() & 0x7F is below ((counter - 1) << 5) & 0xFF: never at a count of 1, always at a count of 5. Then BtlSlotStatusAnimationSet(slot) (btl_slot.c) picks an animation number by the status bits (0x14 to 0x1B for a party slot; 3, 4, 5, 0x10 or 0x11 for another), calls BtlAnimationSet with it and stores it as the slot's kept animation. An active slot then gets hp back: 10 hundredths of its maximum (the stats' +2) when BtlTargetTraitCheck(0, 0x1D, 0, 0) (btl_slot.c) answers 1, which for a party slot means that one of the six bytes at +0x28 of its stats is 0x1D and for any other slot that its byte +0x1B is; 5 more for a party slot whose stats' +0x1E has the bit 0x01; and, when either holds, rng_mask_below(3, 4) on top, a draw of 0 to 3. The hp stops at the maximum, the amount goes to g_BtlSlotAmounts and 5 to g_BtlSlotAmountKinds, and when any slot got some BtlAmountRecordsRun (btl_amount.c) runs frames while the numbers are shown. (4) For each active party slot: status bit 0x10 turns the status into 0x20 with animation 0x18; otherwise status bit 0x20 turns it into 0x30 with animation 0x19 and sets the slot's active byte to 0. (5) For each party slot whose status has the bit 0x01, active or not: the amount is its maximum hp times the byte g_BtlPartyStatus1Shares[slot], over 100; it goes to g_BtlSlotAmounts, with 1 in g_BtlSlotAmountKinds. BtlTargetStatus1Set (btl_status.c) sets that byte to 0xA where it gives a slot the status. BtlAmountRecordsRun shows the numbers, and when a slot was marked g_BtlFallDone is set to 0 and BtlFallRun and BtlItem83Revive (btl_fall.c) are called: the first sets a marked party slot's hp, status and active byte to 0. (6) The six tables of (3) are set to 0 for all 14 slots again, and g_BtlTargetSlot to 0. Its one call is in BtlRun, in every round, after BtlSlot5ReviveTry; BtlRun asks BtlEndCheck (btl_fall.c) right after it whether a side has no active slot left

For each active slot (its byte of g_BtlSlotActiveFlags not 0), from slot 0 on, or from slot 6 on when g_BtlPartyMode is 2, whose 16-bit word at +0x14 of its stats has neither bit of 0xC00 (bits 0x04 and 0x08 of the status, the byte at +0x15), the key is the 16-bit word at +0xC of the stats; the highest of these keys is kept. The 14 keys are then sorted highest first by exchanges, and the order bytes are exchanged with them; a slot that is not active keeps the key 0 and the order byte 0. A loop of 14 passes with an empty body ends the function. Its one call is in BtlTurnOrderRun, which runs the entries of the order one after another and stops at the first 0. BtlMenuCursorMove = 0x80048D2C; // type:func src:coined on:2026-10-13 was:func_80048D2C ev: read in btl_command.c: works out where the pad moves a cursor over items laid out in rows (arguments: a pad record, the items, the number of columns, the number of rows, the cursor; returns the new cursor as a byte; it stores nothing and calls nothing). The items are 12 bytes each, item n standing in column n modulo the columns of row n divided by the columns, and an item whose byte +0 is 0 is passed over. The cursor comes back as it was unless the record's word at +4 (pressed or repeating) has a bit of 0xF000; the bits are tried in the order 0x8000, 0x2000, 0x1000, and what is left is taken as the fourth direction. 0x8000: one column back in the same row, and from column 0 to the row's last column; when the item there is off, further back to the first that is on or to column 0, and when column 0 is off as well, to the row's last column and back again. 0x2000: the same forwards, from the row's last column to column 0. 0x1000: one row up, and from row 0 to the last row; the fourth direction: one row down, and from the last row to row 0; for both, when the item there is off, back along that row to the first that is on, from column 0 to the row's last column and back once more, and when that ends on column 0 too the cursor stays where it was. The whole function was read. 5 jumps from 5 functions, each of which stores the low byte of the answer in the cursor g_BtlMenuCursor and passes the pad record g_BtlMenuPadRecord and the items at g_BtlMenuItems: BtlMenuFirstStep and BtlMenuPresetStep with 2 columns and 2 rows, BtlMenuKindStep with 3 and 2, BtlMenuSpellStep with 4 and 2, BtlMenuItemStep with 6 and 2. docs/spec/code/subsystems/menu-ui.md calls it the grid's cursor logic

Any other number is turned into the kind and the number that sound_effect_play takes. 1 to 0xA: kind 1, the number less 1. 0xB to 0x82 go by the byte g_SoundMapNumber, the map number that SoundMapSet (this file) keeps when it has the area's bank loaded: when the byte is 0x32 or 0, number 0x82 is kind 2 number 1, 0x18 is kind 1 number 0x17, any other below 0x1F is refused, and 0x1F up is kind 2, the number less 0x1F; for any other byte a number below 0x1F is kind 1, the number less 1, and 0x1F up is refused. 0x83 to 0x12A are refused when the byte is 0; otherwise the number is looked for in the id table, the sixteen 16-bit words at g_SoundIds that sound_id_table_set fills, and its place there is the number of kind 3; when it is not in the table the function returns 2 and plays nothing. With direction 1 by key from the largest; with any other by key from the smallest; two pairs whose keys are equal go in order of their second number from the smallest, in both directions. It makes n passes, each comparing pairs i and i + 1 for i from 0 to one less than the count still unsorted and exchanging them when they are out of order: the shape of the textbook bubble sort.
